facts.value: Mid-Year Treasury Management Report 2025-26. Covers the period 1 April to 30 September 2025. Report to Audit Committee, 24 February 2026. Twelve-page paper (Part A cover + Appendix 1 body). Adviser: Arlingclose Limited. Report author: Robert Thurlow, Chief Accountant (robert.thurlow@threerivers.gov.uk — Watford BC and Three Rivers DC operate a shared finance service, hence the @threerivers.gov.uk address on the Watford paper). Report approved by: Michelle Howell, Interim Head of Finance. Chief Finance Officer commentary at 5.1.1. Council received TMS approval on 28 January 2025.

source.title: Mid-Year Treasury Management Report 2025-26 — Audit Committee, 24 February 2026

facts.note: Two documents held on disk: 53108 (Part A cover, 3 pages) and 53109 (Appendix 1 body, ten numbered pages). Together the extraction is complete — the paper is fully self-contained, with balance-sheet, treasury position, loans portfolio, investment position, non-treasury investments, compliance limits and liability benchmark all narrated on-page rather than referred to un-held appendices. Meeting was six months prior to today's date (16 August 2026); the paper remains the last treasury paper on the Modern Gov agenda for the Audit Committee that we hold.

facts.value: 31.3.25 Actual / 31.3.26 Forecast (Table 1, p.4): General Fund CFR £356.969m / £374.910m. Less Lease Liability (Croxley Business Park) £256.093m / £262.310m. Borrowing CFR £100.876m / £112.600m. External borrowing £22.500m / £36.250m (loans to which the Council is committed; excludes optional refinancing). Internal borrowing £78.376m / £76.350m. Less Balance sheet resources (£105.256m) / (£104.164m). Net Investments £26.880m / £27.814m.
facts.note: The Croxley Business Park lease liability is 72% of the total General Fund CFR (256.093 / 356.969 at 31.3.25) — this is a very large IFRS 16-type lease that dominates the balance sheet in headline terms while contributing nothing to the borrowing side. Table 1's presentation is unusually clean because it splits the lease liability out from the borrowing CFR line, making the reconciliation transparent — most councils in the library either bury the lease inside the CFR line or omit the split.

facts.value: Table 2 (p.4). 31.3.25 → 30.9.25 movements. Long-term borrowing PWLB: (£22.500m) → (£16.875m), movement +£5.625m (i.e. reduction in debt), 30.9.25 rate 4.31%. DMADF: £15.700m → £9.000m, movement (£6.700m), rate 3.96%. Cash and cash equivalents: £10.000m → £8.200m, movement (£0.800m), rate 3.77%. Total investments: £25.700m → £17.200m. Net (borrowing)/investments: £3.200m → £0.325m. Reduction in long-term borrowing due to maturity of one loan at £5m and instalment principal payment on one loan at £0.625m.
facts.note: Net cash position swung from £3.2m net investor at 31.3.25 to just £0.325m at 30.9.25. Investment balances ranged £17.199m to £38.392m across the half year due to timing (paragraph before Table 4). The Council is essentially in balance rather than materially net-investor or net-borrower on the mid-year snapshot.

facts.value: Table 3A + 3B (pp.5-6). At 30.9.25: 6 PWLB loans totalling £16.875m at 4.31% weighted average rate, 2.58 years weighted average maturity. Composition — 5 MATURITY loans at £2.5m each (rates 3.93%, 3.93%, 3.96%, 4.01%, 4.81%; residuals 4.42, 3.71, 2.71, 1.71 and 1.44 years) plus 1 EIP loan at £4.375m outstanding, 4.82%, 3.45 years. £5.625m reduction from 31.3.25 comprised £5m of maturity plus £0.625m EIP instalment.
facts.note: Every loan the paper lists at 30.9.25 is identifiable in our price-book file by rate, principal and maturity date. See the loan_book_reconciliation fact and the internal block for the mapping.

facts.value: Paragraph 3.6 (Part A, p.2) states: 'There was no new borrowing during the period, but new borrowing of £20m is anticipated to be required before the end of the 2025-26 financial year. The cost of new borrowing will fall within existing budgets.' Table 1's 31.3.26 forecast external borrowing of £36.250m is consistent with £16.875m at 30.9.25 plus the £20m addition, less around £0.625m of further EIP amortisation.

source.title: Part A paragraph 3.6, p.2; Table 1 external borrowing forecast column, p.4

facts.note: Both £20m tranches now sit in our price-book file — see loan_book_reconciliation. This is a mid-year forecast that landed to the pound.

facts.value: TIES. price_book.py --find 'Watford' returns 'WATFORD BOROUGH COUNCIL'. price_book.py against that borrower (as at 2026-08-16) returns 8 PWLB loans totalling £36,250,000 at a weighted 4.3662% (5 MATURITY, 3 EIP). This matches the paper's Table 1 forecast of £36.250m external borrowing at 31.3.26 to the pound. The six loans that were live at 30 September (paper's Table 3B, £16.875m at 4.31%) all map to individual loans in the file by rate, principal and maturity date. The two additional loans in the file (loan numbers 900882 and 909261, £10m each at 4.57% and 4.29% respectively, both EIP) correspond to the £20m of new borrowing that paragraph 3.6 said was anticipated before year end.

source.title: PWLBtoday price_book.py against paper Tables 1, 3A, 3B and paragraph 3.6

facts.note: Three-way tie. (1) Today's file total £36,250,000 ties Table 1's forecast £36.250m for 31.3.26 to the pound. (2) The 6 loans live at 30.9.25 match the six rows in the paper's Table 3B by rate/principal/maturity — see internal block for the numbered mapping. (3) The remaining £20m in our file corresponds to paragraph 3.6's £20m anticipated new borrowing. The new-money rates were 4.29% (2.5-year EIP maturing 26 July 2028) and 4.57% (5-year EIP maturing 31 January 2031). The Start dates on our file for those two loans are 3 February and 3 March 2026 respectively but per project guidance the file's Start field is not treated as a reliable drawdown date — the email says 'drawn in early 2026' rather than quoting a specific day.

facts.value: TIES to the pound both years. Identity: General Fund CFR − external borrowing − lease liability = internal borrowing. 31.3.25 actual: 356.969 − 22.500 − 256.093 = 78.376 vs paper's 78.376 ✓. 31.3.26 forecast: 374.910 − 36.250 − 262.310 = 76.350 vs paper's 76.350 ✓. Equivalent formulation using Borrowing CFR: 31.3.25 100.876 − 22.500 = 78.376 ✓; 31.3.26 112.600 − 36.250 = 76.350 ✓. Internal borrowing represents 77.7% of Borrowing CFR at 31.3.25 (78.376/100.876) falling to 67.8% at 31.3.26 forecast (76.350/112.600).

source.title: Table 1, p.4 — arithmetic verified against extracted paper text

facts.value: Maturity Structure of Borrowing (p.9) at 30.9.25 actual: Under 12 months 7.41%. 12 months and within 24 months 37.04%. 24 months and within 5 years 55.56%. Upper limit for each bucket is 0% and lower limit 100% (i.e. unconstrained). All within limits. No principal in any bucket beyond 5 years. Weighted average maturity at 30.9.25 = 2.58 years (Table 3A).

source.title: Prudential Indicator 2 — Maturity Structure of Borrowing, p.9

facts.note: 100% of the PWLB book matures within 5 years — the paper's maturity indicator table simply omits the 5-10, 10-20, 20-30, 30-40 and 40-50 buckets because none exists. This is unusual: the standard PWLB tail runs to 30 or 50 years, so a book that fits entirely under a five-year fence is a distinctive shape. On our file today (post the £20m new borrowing), the book still sits entirely under five years — new tranches maturing 2028 and 2031, so nothing beyond January 2031.

facts.value: Liability benchmark table (pp.8-9). Loans CFR: 100.966 (31.3.25) → 112.612 → 121.489 → 124.237 (31.3.28). Balance sheet resources: (105.256) → (104.164) → (78.309) → (76.554). Net loans requirement: (4.290) → 8.448 → 43.181 → 47.683. Plus liquidity allowance £10.0m each year. Liability benchmark: 5.710 → 18.448 → 53.181 → 57.683. Existing borrowing: 22.500 → 36.250 → 50.500 → 64.750. Underlying capital-expenditure funded by borrowing assumption: £12.203m in 2025/26, £9.342m in 2026/27, £3.280m in 2027/28. MRP based on 45-year asset life; income/expenditure/reserves inflation 2.5% p.a.
facts.note: Existing borrowing sits ABOVE the liability benchmark at 31.3.25, 31.3.26 and 31.3.28 — the only year the two roughly cross is 31.3.27 (existing £50.500m vs LB £53.181m, a £2.7m dip below). At 31.3.28 existing borrowing exceeds the LB by £7.067m. The paper flags that borrowing 'significantly above' the LB carries higher risk but does not draw a conclusion; the shape here is modest over-hedging rather than the substantial internal-borrowing crossing many other councils in the library face. The paper's LB chart is on p.9 but the extracted text does not render the graphic — the numerical trajectory is what the email discusses.

facts.value: External Context section (p.5). PWLB certainty rate for 10-year maturity loans: 5.38% at start of period, 5.53% at end; range 5.17% to 5.62%. 20-year maturity: range 5.71% to 6.30%. 50-year maturity: range 5.46% to 6.14%. LA-to-LA short-term borrowing similar to Base Rate at 4.0% to 4.5%. 10-year gilt started 4.65% ended 4.70%, range 4.45% to 4.82%. 20-year gilt started 5.18% ended 5.39%, range 5.10% to 5.55%. SONIA averaged 4.19% over the six months.

source.title: External Context and Borrowing Strategy sections, pp.1-5

facts.note: The paper quotes CERTAINTY rates for PWLB — which is the correct basis for a council eligible for the 0.20% discount. The two new-money EIP rates (4.29% and 4.57%) sit well below the 10-year certainty range because both are short-tenor EIPs — the market prices them off a much shorter part of the certainty curve than the 10-year point, hence a rate closer to 1-3 year money. This is the mechanics point the email makes explicitly.

facts.value: Table 4 (p.6). At 30.9.25: Banks and building societies (unsecured) £8.200m at 3.77% (WAM 1 day); DMADF £9.000m at 3.96% (WAM 7 days); total £17.200m at (aggregate) 7.73% income return, WAM 4 days. Investment balances ranged £17.199m to £38.392m across the half year. Bank Rate cut from 4.50% to 4.25% in May 2025 and to 4.00% in August 2025. DMADF deposit rates ranged 3.90% to 4.55%. Investment limits (Table 7, p.8): single-organisation limit £10m, actual maximum £9.625m at £8.200m at 30.9.25 (complied); own banker limit £10m, actual £9.625m at £8.200m (complied); MMF limit £5m, actual £0m (no MMF exposure).

source.title: Table 4 Treasury Investment Position, p.6; Table 7 Investment Limits, p.8

facts.note: Very short book — WAM 4 days at 30.9.25 versus Arlingclose peer 'Similar LAs' WAM of 53 days (Table 5, p.7). Investment return 3.87% vs peer 4.62% (Table 5). Paper is explicit that the low return is a consequence of the very short duration, which itself reflects the internal-borrowing-first strategy: cash is held for liquidity rather than yield because it is essentially borrowed cash the council needs available. This is not a finding to raise as a criticism — it is a deliberate consequence of the paragraph 3.4 strategy and the paper says as much at paragraphs 3.5 and 3.6 of Part A and in the paragraph before Table 5.

facts.value: Non-Treasury Investments (p.7): £22.461m total. Equity in Hart Homes Watford Ltd £2.400m; Loans to Hart Homes Watford Ltd £11.301m; Loan to West Herts Hospital Trust (Infrastructure) £2.000m; Watford Health Campus Partnership Loan Notes £6.352m; Other immaterial investments £0.408m. Council has no new plans to borrow to invest primarily for financial return (p.5).

Table 8 (p.8) Debt limits. Borrowing 30.9.25 actual £16.875m, 2025/26 maximum £22.500m, Operational Boundary £50.000m, Authorised Limit £60.000m — complied. Finance Leases 30.9.25 actual £256.093m, maximum £256.093m, Operational Boundary £275.000m, Authorised Limit £300.000m — complied. Total debt Operational Boundary £325.000m, Authorised Limit £360.000m — complied. Paper notes the Operational Boundary published in the Capital Strategy 2025/26 was incorrect; revised indicator agreed by Council when 2026/27 strategy set (footnote to Table 8). Long-term treasury investments (p.10): limits £20m in 25/26, 26/27, 27/28 and no fixed date; actual £0 across all — complied. Liquidity indicator (p.10): cash within 1 week actual £17.2m against £1.0m target — complied.

source.title: Compliance section, Tables 7-8, and Additional Indicators, pp.8-10

facts.note: All limits within tolerance. The prior-year operational boundary error is a footnote disclosure and has been corrected in the 2026/27 strategy — not a live compliance issue. Cash within 1 week (£17.2m) is essentially the whole investment book because everything is instant-access or 7-day DMADF.

officer.body:
Dear Robert,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book kept in step with the DMO and priced daily against the premature repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at https://pwlbtoday.org/brochure. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are some thoughts on your Mid-Year Treasury Management Report that Audit Committee received on 24 February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Table 1 in your report is one of the cleaner presentations we've read: splitting the Croxley Business Park lease liability out from the Borrowing CFR is a courtesy most councils don't extend to the reader, and it made the reconciliation below straightforward.

Your paragraph 3.6 said £20m of new borrowing was anticipated before the end of 2025-26. Both tranches now sit in our file: a £10m EIP at 4.29% maturing 26 July 2028 and a £10m EIP at 4.57% maturing 31 January 2031, drawn in early 2026. Together with the six loans running at 30 September that gives 8 PWLB loans totalling £36,250,000 at a weighted 4.37% — which is exactly the £36.250m your Table 1 forecast column carries for 31 March 2026. The six pre-existing loans map one-for-one to Table 3B by rate, principal and maturity, and the £20m addition matches paragraph 3.6 to the pound. It's a paper where the mid-year forecast lands where it said it would.

The point worth flagging is the shape. At 30 September your maturity structure had 100% of the book inside five years — 7.41% under 12 months, 37.04% at 12-24 months, 55.56% at 24-60 months — with a weighted average maturity of 2.58 years. The two new EIPs add amortising principal but nothing beyond January 2031, so on our file today the whole book still reprices inside five years. That's a distinctive shape: the standard PWLB tail in the library runs to 30 or 50 years, and your prudential-indicator table simply omits the longer buckets because none exists. The paragraph 3.4 strategy — 'deferring new borrowing while it has sufficient liquidity' and, longer-term, 'the Council will need to externalise debt' — is doing exactly what it says, and this is the visible shape of that over successive draws.

The two new-money rates are worth reading against your own reference. You quote 10-year PWLB certainty at 5.17% to 5.62% across the period. Both new draws are EIP with average lives roughly half their tenor, so the market prices them off a much shorter part of the curve — hence 4.29% on the 2028 tail and 4.57% on the 2031 tail rather than a 10-year number. On the £16.875m fixed book at 30 September, the same shape carries the 4.31% weighted rate in Table 3A even though the underlying loans were drawn when 10-year rates were higher. Our page at https://pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity carries the daily draws the sector is taking, so the comparison with peers doing the same is easy to run.

One cross-check worth mentioning because it caught nothing to correct. The balance-sheet identity ties to the pound both years: General Fund CFR less external borrowing less lease liability equals your internal-borrowing line exactly — £356.969m less £22.500m less £256.093m equals £78.376m at 31 March 2025, and the same arithmetic on the forecast column gives £76.350m at 31 March 2026. Internal borrowing sits at 78% of the Borrowing CFR at 31 March 2025, falling to 68% at 31 March 2026 forecast — the direction your paragraph 3.4 sets out, moving at the pace it implies.

On training, three courses fit what the paper describes. EIP versus maturity: rate mechanics pairs directly with your two new draws and their rates against your quoted certainty range. The liability benchmark, made practical is worth a look given CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put the benchmark in front of every S151, and your page 9 chart already treats it seriously. Internal borrowing and the point of externalisation fits paragraph 3.4 word for word. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at https://pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts are open to the whole team.

If any of this turns out to be useful, mentioning it to colleagues or neighbours would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
